seoTitle: Paris Travel Guide: Top Things to Do, Neighborhoods, and Day Trips
seoDescription: Explore Paris through specific landmarks, museums, historic districts and practical planning context, with major POIs tied to the Seine and the city's walkable neighborhoods.
intro: Paris grew around the Seine, and the river remains the clearest way to understand the relationship among the historic core, royal and civic monuments, major museums and later neighborhoods. The Île de la Cité anchors the medieval city, while the Louvre, Tuileries and Champs-Élysées trace a monumental axis westward through centuries of urban change. Plan by geographic cluster rather than landmark count: reserve the high-demand interiors, then walk the streets, gardens and riverbanks that connect them.

topThings.title: Eiffel Tower and Champ de Mars
topThings.description: The Eiffel Tower was completed for the 1889 Exposition Universelle and rises above the Champ de Mars on the Left Bank. Its observation levels provide a broad view of the Seine, the city's radiating avenues and the dense roofscape that is difficult to appreciate from street level. Pair the tower with the lawns and riverfront rather than treating it as a stand-alone photo stop.

topThings.title: Louvre Museum
topThings.description: The Louvre occupies a former royal palace whose courtyards and wings record centuries of expansion before the building became a public museum during the French Revolution. Its collections range from ancient civilizations to European painting and sculpture, including works such as the Mona Lisa and Winged Victory of Samothrace. Choose a wing or collection in advance because the museum is too large for a useful all-at-once visit.

topThings.title: Musée d’Orsay
topThings.description: The Musée d’Orsay occupies the former Gare d'Orsay, a Beaux-Arts railway station built for the 1900 Exposition Universelle. The museum is especially strong in nineteenth-century French art, including major Impressionist and Post-Impressionist collections by Monet, Degas, Renoir and Van Gogh. The converted station and its large clock faces make the building itself part of the experience.

topThings.title: Notre-Dame Cathedral and Île de la Cité
topThings.description: Notre-Dame stands on the Île de la Cité, the island at the historic core of Paris, and represents several centuries of Gothic construction beginning in the twelfth century. The cathedral reopened after the extensive restoration that followed the 2019 fire, while the surrounding island still contains the street pattern, bridges and institutions of the city's oldest center. Continue on foot to Sainte-Chapelle and the Seine quays to keep the medieval geography intact.

topThings.title: Sainte-Chapelle
topThings.description: Sainte-Chapelle was built in the thirteenth century within the medieval royal palace on the Île de la Cité. Its upper chapel is enclosed by exceptionally tall stained-glass windows that turn the interior into one of the clearest surviving statements of Rayonnant Gothic design. Because it sits close to Notre-Dame, the two monuments fit naturally into one focused historic-core walk.

topThings.title: Montmartre and Sacré-Cœur
topThings.description: Montmartre rises on a hill north of central Paris and developed a distinct identity through its former village streets, entertainment venues and late nineteenth-century artist community. Sacré-Cœur crowns the summit and provides a broad south-facing view over the city from its forecourt. Walk beyond the busiest approach streets to see how steep lanes, small squares and older buildings give the district its topographic character.

topThings.title: Arc de Triomphe
topThings.description: The Arc de Triomphe stands at the center of Place Charles de Gaulle, where twelve avenues radiate outward in one of Paris's most recognizable pieces of urban planning. Commissioned by Napoleon and completed in the nineteenth century, the monument also contains the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath its arch. The rooftop view is especially useful for understanding the Champs-Élysées and the city's long east-west axes.

topThings.title: Luxembourg Gardens
topThings.description: The Luxembourg Gardens spread around the Luxembourg Palace on the Left Bank and combine formal French layouts with shaded promenades, lawns, sculpture and a central basin. Created in the seventeenth century for Marie de' Medici, the grounds remain one of central Paris's most important everyday public spaces. They provide a slower counterpoint to museum-heavy sightseeing and connect naturally with the Latin Quarter and Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

neighborhoods: Le Marais for medieval street fragments, hôtels particuliers, museums, galleries and an active Jewish quarter.
Saint-Germain-des-Prés for Left Bank literary history, churches, cafés and easy access to the Seine.
Latin Quarter for the Sorbonne, Roman and medieval traces, bookshops and steep streets rising from the river.
Canal Saint-Martin for nineteenth-century waterways, neighborhood cafés and a more residential eastern-Paris rhythm.
Montmartre for hilltop views, former village streets and the artistic history surrounding Place du Tertre and Sacré-Cœur.
whenToGo: Late spring and early autumn usually provide comfortable temperatures and long enough days for walking between districts.
Summer brings the heaviest pressure at headline monuments, so timed reservations and early starts become more important.
Winter is colder and darker but can be effective for museum-focused trips and quieter neighborhood walks.
gettingAround: Use the Metro for cross-city movement, but walk within each district so the relationship among monuments, streets and the Seine remains visible.
Group sights by arrondissement or adjoining neighborhoods to avoid spending the day underground moving between distant reservations.
Use RER trains for farther destinations such as Versailles and for selected airport connections; check current service before departure.
dayTrips: Versailles for the former royal palace, formal gardens and a direct regional-rail connection from central Paris.
Giverny for Claude Monet's house and gardens during the main flowering season.
Reims for its Gothic cathedral and the historic Champagne houses of northeastern France.
Fontainebleau for the château and the extensive forest surrounding the town.
Provins for medieval walls, towers and a compact historic townscape southeast of Paris.
